title: Monolith Systems - Redwood POC scoping (capacity & autoscale)
summary: POC scoping call to define success criteria, workload sizing, and autoscaling strategy for a 6-week POC. Primary goals: validate latency SLOs under peak traffic, measure cost/per-token with reserved GPUs + burst to on-demand, and test fallback policies to smaller model variants. Action items include benchmark scripts, sample payloads, pricing deck, and scheduling a two-day benchmark run.
next_steps: Redwood to send POC pricing options (reserved GPU tiers + burst pricing) by 2026-12-11
Monolith to share expected traffic profile and sample dataset by 2026-12-12
Priya to propose benchmark script and baseline model config by 2026-12-13
Schedule 2-day benchmark run for week of 2026-12-14 (Alex to coordinate)
Redwood to provide SOC2 & security docs and VPC deployment notes
action_items: Alex Chen: send pricing deck + reserved GPU options by 2026-12-11
Priya Kapoor: share benchmark harness + baseline config by 2026-12-13
Samir Patel: provide sample payloads and 7-day peak QPS profile by 2026-12-12
Jordan Myers: confirm network egress and VPC requirements by 2026-12-14
Rebecca Li: define POC success criteria (latency SLO, quality thresholds) by 2026-12-13
header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Time: 15:00 - 15:52 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Monolith Eng Lead), Rebecca Li (Monolith Head of ML), Jordan Myers (Monolith Infra), Tara Gomez (Procurement), Evan Park (SRE)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Samir Patel (Monolith): Hey Alex, Samir here. Rebecca, Jordan and Tara are on.
[00:09] Rebecca Li (Monolith): Rebecca on my side.
[00:11] Jordan Myers (Monolith): Jordan here.
[00:13] Tara Gomez (Monolith): Tara, thanks.
[00:15] Alex Chen (Redwood): Great. Priya and Diego from our side. Agenda: scope the POC - success criteria, workload sizing, reserved capacity and burst, fallback policies, and timeline. Sound good?
[00:24] Rebecca: Yep, that's what we need. We're looking to validate inference economics and latencies for our Summarize+Search feature. Key is sub-200ms median for short prompts and under 500ms p95 for longer sessions, while keeping costs under our internal target.
[00:36] Priya Kapoor (Redwood): Thanks Rebecca. Can you give us a sense of expected concurrency and tokens per request?
[00:42] Samir: Sure. Typical interactive user flow is 10-50 tokens for a summary, but we have an extraction step that can be 200-400 tokens. Traffic wise, baseline is ~150 concurrent requests during business hours, peaks up to 800 concurrent for flash events. QPS distribution is spiky - 80% short requests, 20% long.
[01:03] Diego Morales (Redwood): Helpful. Do you have any current numbers on tokens/sec or throughput from your in-house setup?
[01:08] Samir: We measured a local run with a single A100 equivalent, roughly 120 tokens/sec for the long path, about 600 tokens/sec for short prompts. But our baseline infra isn't optimized - so take those with caution.
[01:20] Rebecca: Also, quality matters. We want to pin to the new open model you recommend, but need to compare outputs between the full FP16 and a quantized variant. Latency/quality tradeoff is a success axis.
[01:33] Priya: Understood. For the POC we usually suggest a reserved GPU pool sized to cover typical baseline traffic with headroom, then allow burst to on-demand instances for peaks. That keeps predictable unit costs. For your numbers - baseline 150 conc - I'd propose reserving capacity equivalent to 4x A100-class GPUs to cover baseline with continuous batching, and enable burst up to 12 GPUs for peaks.
[01:54] Jordan: That burst sounds right but we're concerned about cold-starts and multi-tenant fallback. How does Redwood handle fallback if burst capacity isn't available?
[02:01] Alex: Good question. Our typical POC pattern: 1) try reserved pool, 2) if queue grows beyond threshold, spin up burst nodes (on-demand) in the same region, 3) if burst cap reached, gracefully downgrade to a compatible, smaller quantized model that reduces latency and token cost, and optionally route to a hosted (SaaS) fallback endpoint if private capacity is exhausted. We can set policies and thresholds.
[02:26] Evan Park (Monolith): Routing to hosted is a compliance question for us - data residency and redaction are concerns. We'd need to see the VPC/private deployment flow.
[02:34] Alex: Absolutely. For POC we can run the control plane in Redwood's cloud but keep inference in your VPC with private connectors. We also offer an on-prem package if required. We'll send security docs.
[02:45] Tara Gomez (Procurement): For budgeting, we need both a reserved monthly commit price and burst unit pricing. Also clarify SLA differences for reserved vs. burst.
[02:54] Alex: We'll include a pricing matrix: reserved monthly price (committed), burst per-hour rate, and estimated unit cost per 1k tokens under each mode. SLA for reserved capacity includes latency SLO targets and uptime; burst is best-effort with softer latency targets.
[03:10] Priya: Back to sizing - Samir mentioned 200-400 token requests at peak. With 4 GPUs for baseline that gives about X throughput - we should confirm with benchmarks. For POC we'll run a workload-shaped benchmark that mirrors your traffic (80/20 short/long) across concurrency levels from 150 to 800. We'll capture median/p95 latency, tokens/sec, and cost per token.
[03:33] Rebecca: What about batching behavior? We don't want 200ms median become 700ms because of batching. Some requests are latency sensitive.
[03:40] Priya: We'll tune batching policies - separate low-latency route for interactive short prompts with small max-batch and strict latency SLO, and a throughput route for long extraction requests that can tolerate slightly higher latency but benefit from batching. That maps to route-level configs in the POC.
[03:56] Samir: How would autoscale be triggered? Time-based? Queue-length? CPU/GPU utilization?
[04:02] Diego: We primarily use request queue length and observed latency. Autoscaler watches queue growth and p95 latency; if p95 exceeds N ms for M seconds, spin up burst nodes. We'll share the exact thresholds in the benchmark run.
[04:14] Jordan: On networking: our VPC has strict egress rules; can the burst nodes be brought up inside our VPC?
[04:20] Alex: Yes, burst within Private mode will spin nodes in your VPC using our agent. For a quick POC we can do private connectors; for full private deployment we use a control-plane-lite approach. Details are in the security doc we'll send.
[04:31] Tara: Any pre-existing integrations we need? SSO or audit log hooks?
[04:35] Priya: We support SAML SSO, SSO provisioning, KMS integrations for key wrapping, and stream audit logs to your SIEM. We'll provide RBAC patterns for the POC.
[04:45] Rebecca: Let's define success criteria now so it's concrete. I propose: 1) median latency for short prompts < 200ms, p95 < 400ms; 2) long prompts median < 400ms, p95 < 700ms; 3) cost per 1k tokens using reserved+burst within 20% of your estimate; 4) successful failover to quantized variant with <2x quality regression (we'll measure automatic evals).
[05:09] Priya: That seems reasonable. We'll include objective evaluation steps: automated eval prompt set and quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE or task-specific scoring).
[05:18] Samir: Timeline? We'd like the POC to run in the next two weeks. Six weeks total: 1 week setup, 2-week benchmark/iteration, 3-week evaluation and integration.
[05:26] Alex: We can do that - proposed start next Tuesday 2026-12-14. Setup week includes access, VPC connector, and initial baseline runs.
[05:33] Diego: For benchmarks we ask you to provide an anonymized sample of payloads and a 7-day traffic histogram. We'll generate the harness and a JMeter-style runner that simulates concurrency and QPS.
[05:44] Jordan: We can share that by Friday. Also, what's your recommended model family? We want something similar quality to the current open LLMs but tuned for latency.
transcript_continued:
[06:01] Priya: For POC we often suggest Redwood-XL (open checkpoint) for baseline and Redwood-XL-quant for fallback. We'll run FP16 and 4-bit quant variants.
[06:10] Rebecca: Will the quant variant be supported by your runtime kernels without large perf regressions?
[06:15] Priya: Yes - our runtime supports quantized kernels and KV cache optimizations. We'll include perf deltas in the benchmark output.
[06:24] Samir: Regarding fallback: you mentioned routing to hosted endpoint - are there data retention and encryption differences?
[06:30] Alex: Hosted path is encrypted in transit and at rest, but it's outside your VPC. If that is unacceptable we won't enable SaaS fallback for production. For the POC we can keep everything in private mode.
[06:42] Evan: For chaos scenarios, if an entire region is degraded, can we reroute to a different region's reserved pool?
[06:48] Diego: Yes, we support smart routing by policy - region failover and a model-compat fallback. We'll test region failover as part of POC if you want.
[06:58] Jordan: That would be useful. Latency will increase but availability is key.
[07:03] Tara: On procurement - we need an estimated cost range for the 6-week POC. Even a ballpark helps.
[07:09] Alex: We'll produce a two-tier estimate: minimal reserved (4 GPUs) + 8 GPU burst cap for peaks and a higher reserved (8 GPUs) option for heavy baseline. For the 6-week POC we'll prorate monthly commit. We'll include best-case/worst-case cost based on your 7-day peak profile.
[07:25] Rebecca: QA metrics - how do we measure 'quality regression under quantization'?
[07:29] Priya: We'll run the eval set (you provide) and compute task-specific metrics and a pass/fail threshold. If the quantized model fails quality thresholds we'll record regression and keep it out of failover.
[07:40] Samir: For benchmarking, will you capture token-level cost and per-route cost?
[07:44] Diego: Yes - the Console shows token-level cost, per-route breakdown, and latency percentiles. We'll give you the benchmark spreadsheet after the run.
[07:53] Evan: Can we run a smoke test internally first? Maybe a single-node baseline to sanity-check configs?
[07:58] Priya: Absolutely. We'll do a baseline single-node perf test the first day to validate config and then run the scaled benchmark.
[08:06] Tara: Contractually, we may need a short MSA or SOW. What's Redwood's standard POC SOW?
[08:12] Alex: We have a POC SOW template covering scope, data handling, and deliverables. We'll attach it with pricing.
[08:18] Rebecca: One more question: how long does it take to spin up burst nodes? We need latency for scaling events documented - e.g., spin-up time from zero to ready.
[08:26] Diego: Typical cold-start is 90-180 seconds for on-demand GPUs depending on image pull and region; warm standby can reduce that to under 30s. For POC we recommend warm warmers for critical routes.
[08:36] Jordan: Warm standby sounds necessary for our flash events. What's the cost tradeoff?
[08:40] Alex: Warm standby is billed at partial rate but gives faster scaling. We'll show cost pro forma.
[08:47] Samir: About autoscaler thresholds - can you provide default configs we can tune?
[08:51] Priya: Yes. Default: scale when queue > 50 requests for 60s or p95 latency > threshold for 30s. We'll provide tunables.
[08:59] Rebecca: For the POC report, can you include a regression dashboard for quality vs latency?
[09:03] Diego: Yes - we'll include charts: median/p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and quality metric deltas across model variants.
closing:
[09:20] Alex Chen (Redwood): Recap: Redwood sends pricing deck, SOW, security docs; Priya sends benchmark harness; Monolith shares sample payloads and traffic histogram; schedule benchmark week of 2026-12-14. Does that reflect?
[09:31] Tara Gomez (Monolith): Yes. We'll look for the docs and confirm internal approvals.
[09:35] Rebecca Li (Monolith): Looking forward to the benchmark.
[09:38] Alex Chen (Redwood): Great - thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the materials.
[09:42] Meeting ended.
notes: Proposed reserved pool: 4 GPUs baseline, burst up to 12 GPUs (on-demand)
Split routes for low-latency short prompts vs throughput long prompts
Fallback order: reserved -> burst -> quantized model -> hosted SaaS endpoint (optional)
Benchmark metrics: median/p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, quality regression metrics
